title: From food enrichment to additive manufacturing: process–structure–property relationships of Atomet 195 SP water-atomized pure iron powder fabricated via laser powder bed fusion

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Metal additive manufacturing, and in particular laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF), has enabled the fabrication of metallic components with complex geometries and thin-walled features that are difficult or impossible to achieve using conventional manufacturing routes [ 1 ,  2 ,  3 ,  4 ,  5 – 6 ]. Owing to its layer-wise nature and localized melting–solidification cycles, L-PBF offers substantial freedom in controlling part geometry, microstructure, and local material properties [ 7 ,  8 ,  9 ,  10 ,  11 – 12 ]. More broadly, recent metallic additive manufacturing studies have also shown that feedstock selection, process route, local thermal history, and deposition strategy strongly influence microstructure formation and mechanical performance [ 13 ,  14 ,  15 – 16 ]. In the biomedical field, these capabilities are particularly relevant for the development of biodegradable temporary implants, where control over geometry and material distribution can be used to tailor mechanical response and degradation behavior [ 17 ,  18 ]. Among biodegradable metallic materials, pure iron has emerged as a promising candidate for temporary orthopedic applications due to its excellent biocompatibility, non-toxicity of degradation products, and favorable mechanical strength compared to magnesium- and zinc-based systems [ 19 ,  20 ,  21 ,  22 – 23 ].

Despite these advantages, pure iron presents two major limitations for biodegradable implant applications. First, its degradation rate in physiological environments is generally slow, which may delay implant resorption beyond the required tissue-healing period. Second, the elastic modulus of dense pure iron is substantially higher than that of cortical and trabecular bone, increasing the risk of stress shielding when fully dense components are used [ 23 ,  24 ]. These limitations demand careful control of geometry, porosity, surface area, and microstructure to achieve clinically relevant mechanical and degradation behavior. L-PBF is therefore particularly relevant not only for producing dense reference materials, but also as a route toward porous and lattice-based architectures capable of reducing apparent stiffness and increasing surface area. However, the realization of such application-driven architectures requires, as a prerequisite, the establishment of reliable and reproducible L-PBF processing conditions for the candidate feedstock material.

Despite the growing number of studies on L-PBF processing of pure iron, defining processing conditions that remain robust against variations in individual process parameters continues to be a challenge [ 3 ,  4 ,  25 ,  26 – 27 ]. Volumetric energy density is frequently employed as a simplified descriptor to rationalize processing behavior; however, identical energy density values can be achieved through different combinations of laser power, scanning speed, hatch spacing, and beam characteristics, potentially giving rise to distinct melt pool dynamics, defect populations, and microstructural features [ 28 ,  29 ,  30 – 31 ]. Consequently, parameter sets selected solely on the basis of energy density or single performance metrics may exhibit limited robustness when modest variations in processing conditions are introduced. A systematic assessment of process parameter interactions and their influence on densification, mechanical response, and microstructural development is therefore essential, particularly when introducing new powder grades or atomization routes.

Most L-PBF studies on pure iron have employed gas-atomized powders [ 32 ,  33 ,  34 ,  35 ,  36 – 37 ], which offer spherical morphologies, narrow size distributions, low oxygen content, and favorable flowability. However, gas-atomized powders are typically more expensive than water-atomized alternatives, which can limit their attractiveness for cost-sensitive applications and early-stage biomedical process development. This issue is particularly relevant for biodegradable implant research, where patient-specific designs, porous scaffolds, and lattice architectures often require iterative parameter development, small-batch fabrication, and extensive mechanical and biological validation. Reducing feedstock cost can therefore lower the barrier to material screening and process optimization before application-specific implant geometries are produced.

Water-atomized powders provide a lower-cost alternative, though with recognized trade-offs: irregular morphologies, broader size distributions, reduced flowability and packing density, and potentially higher oxygen content [ 37 ,  38 ,  39 ,  40 – 41 ], all of which can affect powder-bed uniformity, melt pool stability, oxide incorporation, and final part properties [ 42 ]. Therefore, the lower cost of water-atomized powders is only useful for biomedical additive manufacturing if reliable processing windows can be established despite these powder-related limitations. Only a limited number of studies have explored water-atomized iron feedstocks for L-PBF. Letenneur et al. [ 43 ] and Paloušek et al. [ 44 ] investigated Atomet FeAM, a water-atomized iron powder no longer commercially available, while Im et al. [ 45 ] employed a partially pre-alloyed water-atomized system. Lopes et al. [ 46 ] recently provided a comprehensive parametric study of Atomet FeAM on the same L-PBF system used in the present work; however, the discontinuation of this powder limits the transferability of those findings. An overview of existing literature on L-PBF processing of pure iron is provided in Table  1 .

The present study introduces Atomet 195 SP (Rio Tinto, Canada) to laser powder bed fusion. Atomet 195 SP is a high-purity water-atomized iron powder commercially produced for food enrichment, pharmaceutical-related, and other non-structural applications, and has not previously been evaluated for L-PBF [ 47 ,  48 ]. Its relevance in the present work lies in the combination of high purity, commercial availability, and potential cost advantage compared with specialty gas-atomized AM feedstocks. However, its commercial use in food or pharmaceutical-related sectors should not be interpreted as evidence of medical-grade certification or direct implant suitability. Instead, the powder is investigated here as a candidate low-cost feedstock for L-PBF process development of pure iron. Although both Atomet FeAM and Atomet 195 SP are water-atomized pure iron powders from the same manufacturer, differences in particle size distribution, morphology, flowability, packing behavior, and surface chemistry preclude the direct transfer of previously established processing parameters. This is consistent with the broader understanding that even nominally similar powder grades within the same material system can yield measurably different consolidation behavior, defect populations, and mechanical response when processed by L-PBF [ 4 ,  25 ,  42 ,  46 ,  49 ], necessitating dedicated process development for each new feedstock.

To address this, a Taguchi L16 orthogonal array was employed to evaluate the influence of scanning speed, hatch spacing, and laser spot size on densification behavior, surface quality, microstructure, and mechanical response across a volumetric energy density range of 34.09–120.00J mm −3 . Two complementary analytical approaches were adopted: (i) statistical assessment of individual process parameter effects using signal-to-noise (S/N) analysis and analysis of variance (ANOVA), and (ii) evaluation of property evolution as a function of volumetric energy density, including deliberate comparison of different parameter combinations yielding identical energy density values. The characterization scope extends beyond typical parameter screening studies to include porosity quantification in both horizontal and vertical build planes, surface roughness, Vickers hardness in both orientations, full tensile testing, fractographic analysis, and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) on multiple specimens fabricated with different parameter combinations at the same nominal energy density—directly addressing the limitation of volumetric energy density as a sole process descriptor. This combined approach enables the identification of a robust processing window and the underlying process–structure–property relationships for this previously untested feedstock. Establishing this baseline is a necessary prerequisite for subsequent studies on porous architectures, degradation/corrosion behavior, and biological performance, since application-specific evaluations require reproducible processing conditions and a clear understanding of how process parameters affect defect formation, surface quality, microstructure, and mechanical response. sections.heading: Powder characterization
paragraphs: The morphology of the Atomet 195 SP iron powder was characterized using a Phenom XL (G2+EDX+SED) scanning electron microscope. The particle size distribution was determined by laser diffraction using a Coulter LS 230 particle size analyzer. The tapped density was measured using a Copley JV 110i tap density tester in accordance with ISO 3953 [ 55 ]; a 50 g mass of powder was placed in the measurement cylinder and subjected to 600 taps at a rate of 300 taps per minute. The true density was evaluated by helium pycnometry. Powder flowability was assessed using a Hall flowmeter funnel in accordance with ASTM B213 [ 56 ].

The nominal chemical composition and particle size classification of Atomet 195 SP were taken from the supplier datasheet [ 48 ]. According to the datasheet, Atomet 195 SP consists of Fe balance, 0.01 wt% C, 0.08 wt% O, and 0.007 wt% S. The supplier-reported particle size classification indicates 98 wt% below 45 μm, with 2 wt% between 45 μm to 150 μm and only trace fractions above 150 μm. Nitrogen content was not reported in the supplier datasheet and was not independently measured in the present study.

sections.heading: L-PBF process
Surface roughness, tensile testing and fracture analysis
Porosity measurement and indentation tests
paragraphs: Parallelepipedic specimens were prepared to evaluate porosity in the horizontal plane, while cylindrical specimens were sectioned to assess porosity in the vertical plane. All samples were ground and polished using standard metallographic procedures to prepare them for analysis. Macrographs of the polished surfaces were acquired using an Emspira 3 (Leica, Germany) digital microscope operated with Enersight v3 software. Porosity was quantified using the open-source ImageJ 1.54g software through image thresholding and binarization techniques.
Vickers hardness measurements were performed on the same polished surfaces using a Dia Testor 2 RC hardness tester (Wolpert, Germany) under a 5 kgf load, in accordance with ISO 6507 [ 59 ].

sections.heading: Microstructural characterization
paragraphs: The microstructures of side and top surfaces within fabricated cylindrical and parallelepipedal specimens, respectively, were prepared using standard metallographic procedures and analysed using an Axiophot (Zeiss, Germany) optical microscope under bright-field illumination at magnifications of 100 × and 200 ×. Microstructural images were captured using a DP-22 digital camera (Olympus, Japan), operated with OLYMPUS Stream Basic software. Etching was performed using a 4% Nital solution.

SEM-EBSD analysis was carried out using a FEI QUANTA 400 FEG ESEM microscope. Prior to EBSD acquisition, cross-sections of the specimens were prepared by conventional metallographic procedures. The preparation involved sequential grinding using SiC abrasive papers up to 1000 grit, followed by polishing with 6 μm and 1 μm diamond suspensions. A final polishing step was performed using a 0.3 μm colloidal silica suspension for at least 45 min to reduce surface deformation and improve crystallographic indexing quality.

EBSD maps were acquired at an accelerating voltage of 15 kV, using spot size 5.5, diaphragm aperture 3, low-vacuum mode, and chamber pressures between 30-40Pa. The working distance ranged from 11.7-16.5 mm. EBSD acquisition was performed using a hexagonal grid, an exposure time of 0.03 s, gain values between 10.2 and 10.6, 4 × 4 binning, and a step size of 1.20 μm. The EBSD data were used for inverse pole figure mapping, phase indexing, and grain size analysis.

sections.heading: Powder characteristics
paragraphs: The characteristics of the as-received powder are shown in Fig.  2 . Fig. 2 a  General overview of powder morphology;  b  spherical particle;  c  larger irregular particle;  d  main particle with attached satellite;  e  particle size distribution and cumulative volume fraction of Atomet 195 SP powder;  f  PSD statistics from laser diffraction;  g  supplier-reported sieve classification

SEM images revealed that the powder particles exhibit predominantly irregular morphologies (Fig.  2 a and c), with a minority displaying near-spherical geometries (Fig.  2 b), which is characteristic of water-atomized powders. Additionally, satellite particles were frequently observed adhered to larger primary particles (Fig.  2 d).

sections.heading: Tensile properties, fractographic analysis, and microstructural characterization
paragraphs: The yield point phenomenon in low-carbon ferritic iron is commonly attributed to the pinning of mobile dislocations by interstitial solute atoms, particularly carbon and nitrogen, forming Cottrell atmospheres [ 69 ]. Lejček et al. [ 68 ] confirmed this mechanism for L-PBF pure iron through in-situ TEM deformation experiments and quantified the effective binding energy of carbon to dislocations from the yield drop. In the present study, the progressive attenuation of the yield point with decreasing energy density is consistent with the increasing defect density at lower energy inputs: macroscopic discontinuities act as stress concentrators [ 70 ], initiating localized plastic flow before the bulk pinning forces can be overcome. Although the supplier datasheet reports a carbon content of 0.01 wt% for Atomet 195 SP, nitrogen content was not reported and interstitial element contents were not independently measured after L-PBF processing. Therefore, the observed discontinuous yielding is consistent with Cottrell atmosphere-mediated dislocation pinning in ferritic iron, but the relative contribution of carbon, nitrogen, thermal history, and defect population cannot be quantitatively separated from the present data (Table  8 ).

The evolution of ductility with volumetric energy density is further evidenced by the macroscopic fracture appearance (Fig.  11 ). Specimens fabricated at low energy densities exhibit limited necking and relatively flat fracture surfaces, whereas specimens at higher energy densities show pronounced necking and localized plastic deformation. Fig. 11 Macroscopic fracture morphology of L-PBF-fabricated pure iron tensile specimens at different volumetric energy densities

Representative fractographies are shown in Fig.  12 . At the magnifications used, the fracture surfaces mainly reveal fracture topography and defect morphology rather than fully resolved fine-scale fracture micromechanisms. No dominant cleavage facets or intergranular fracture features were clearly identified, and the macroscopic necking observed at higher energy densities is consistent with a predominantly ductile tensile response. However, individual dimples were not sufficiently resolved to support a quantitative dimple-size analysis. Therefore, the fractographic interpretation is limited to the relationship between pore morphology, defect distribution, necking behavior, and measured ductility. Higher-magnification SEM analysis would be required to conclusively distinguish local microvoid coalescence features from other fine-scale fracture mechanisms.
